angle: The best outbound plays aren't the templated ones. They're the weird, nuanced ones.
post_first_line: Skyler Mickunas: the best signals are weird.
linkedin_post:
Skyler Mickunas: the best signals are weird.

The most successful customer use cases Skyler sees are often the most nuanced, and they rarely come out of a template.

Take Delve, a partner Unify has seen a lot of success with. They want to know whether a target account already has a certain security certification in place.

That isn't an out-of-the-box signal everyone in the audience would find valuable. It's specific to what Delve sells.

That's also why Unify doesn't have a full set of templated use cases. It would be a lot of work, and not all of them would apply to the average user.

Custom signals are a bit of a black box once they're opened up.

The plays that work are built around the one question only your business needs answered.

What's your most niche buying signal?

lesson.title: Niche signals beat generic templates
takeaways: Some of the most successful use cases are the most nuanced ones.
A signal that's valuable to one company may mean nothing to most others.
Templated use cases rarely apply to the average user, so custom signals fill the gap.
lesson.exercise: Write down the one question about a target account that only your business cares about, like whether they're already SOC 2 compliant. Turn it into a custom signal and test it on a small account list.

caption: Weird signals beat templates

angle: We track about 100 signals, but the rep decides what to do with each one
linkedin_post:
We track close to 100 signals.

But we don't tell reps what to do with any of them.

When a company hits a signal, it gets routed to the rep. From there, the rep picks the path.

Sometimes that's an auto email, with phone call and LinkedIn tasks layered in so they can work out of Unify.

Sometimes it's a manual email, where we hand over all the context so the rep can write a sniper shot.

Sometimes it's just a different alert.

Whatever workflow the rep wants, we work backwards from that.

The goal is to maximize our share on each prospect and account. Forcing one motion on every signal doesn't get us there.

Signals tell you when to act. The rep knows how.

How much control do your reps have over signal response?

Slide 4: Option one: auto email plus phone and LinkedIn tasks.

Slide 6: Option three: a different alert, based on rep preference.

Slide 8: The goal: maximize our share of each account.

lesson.title: Let reps choose the play for each signal
takeaways: Routing a signal to a rep is only step one. The response should fit the rep's workflow.
Different signals call for different motions: auto email, manual sniper shot, or an alert.
Working backwards from how reps want to operate helps maximize share on each account.
lesson.exercise: List your top 10 signals. For each, write the response a rep would choose (auto email, manual email, call or LinkedIn task, or alert) and what context they'd need to act.

caption: 100 signals, rep's choice

angle: Our rule: if a rep owns the account, it never goes into an automated play
post_first_line: Around 200 accounts per AE. 500 to 600 per MBR.
linkedin_post:
Around 200 accounts per AE. 500 to 600 per MBR.

At Unify, each AE owns around 200 accounts and each MBR owns 500 to 600. We also have shared accounts by segment, plus an inbound MBR who handles our warmer, inbound-driven signals.

Our automated plays run outside of all that. They look for signals on accounts nobody owns, where Unify could be a good fit.

Our rule: if a rep owns the account, it never goes into an automated play.

Say Audrey, an MBR on our team, owns an account. We don't funnel that account into a sequence. We send Audrey the signal, and Audrey decides what to do with it based on how Audrey likes to work.

Automation is great at finding signals. It's bad at overriding the person who owns the relationship.

Owners get the signal. Automation gets the unowned whitespace.

Where does your automation overlap with rep-owned accounts?

Slide 4: Shared accounts are split by segment
Slide 5: An inbound MBR handles the warmer signals
Slide 6: Automation runs outside all of that ownership
Slide 7: If Audrey owns it, Audrey gets the signal
Slide 8: Account ownership trumps everything else

lesson.title: Let account ownership decide what gets automated
takeaways: Define clear account ownership by role before building any automated play.
Route signals on owned accounts to the owner, not into a sequence.
Point automation at accounts nobody owns, and let reps choose how to act on their own.
lesson.exercise: Export your active automated plays and cross-check the target lists against rep-owned accounts. Remove every overlap and set up a signal alert to the owner instead.

caption: Owned accounts skip automation

angle: Why we tell our AEs not to automate their outreach
post_first_line: Our AEs don't automate their outreach.
linkedin_post:
Our AEs don't automate their outreach.

That's on purpose, and it surprises people.

Skyler Mickunas explains that Unify encourages AEs to avoid automation at the engagement level. Automated plays that pick up new hires at target accounts or other signals are fine. Automated sequences are where it stops.

The reason: AEs have a strong grasp of the value prop and what different decision makers care about. They run a much lower volume of really high converting outreach.

They're also closed lost circle back specialists. When a prospect says the timing is off, an AE sets a reminder. Then the prospect mentions they're hiring a head of demand gen, and that's the moment to reach back out.

If AEs started running automated email sequences, their time would be better spent on what Skyler calls sniper work.

Signals can be automated. The judgment about what to say and when to say it is the part worth keeping human.

Where do you draw the line on automation?

Slide 2: Automate the signals, like new hires at target accounts.
Slide 3: Keep the engagement itself human and deliberate.
Slide 4: AEs know the value prop and what each buyer cares about.
Slide 5: That means lower volume and much higher converting outreach.
Slide 6: Our AEs are closed lost circle back specialists.
Slide 7: Timing off today? Set a reminder for the next trigger.
Slide 8: Sniper work beats automated email sequences for AEs.

lesson.title: Automate the signal, not the conversation
takeaways: Automating signals like new hires at target accounts is encouraged. Automating engagement is not.
AEs who understand the value prop and each decision maker run lower volume, higher converting outreach.
Closed lost deals are worth circling back on when a timing objection turns into a trigger, like a new hire.
lesson.exercise: Review your closed lost deals where timing was the objection. Set a reminder on each one tied to a specific trigger, like a relevant hire, and reach out personally when it fires.

caption: Don't automate your AEs

angle: Pushing reps from 300 to 1,000 accounts a week just makes conversion pay the price
post_first_line: Reps do their best work at 200 to 300 accounts.
linkedin_post:
Reps do their best work at 200 to 300 accounts.

Push past that and something quietly breaks.

Skyler Mickunas laid out the math behind it. Expecting a rep to work 500 to 1,000 accounts a week as diligently as 200 to 300 is naive.

At a certain point, a high volume expectation means conversion on average activity pays the price.

The goal is the outcome, not the activity count. If volume goes up and conversion goes down, the outcome probably doesn't move in any meaningful way.

The math varies case by case. But in general, Skyler's team has reps work about 500 to 600 accounts per month diligently, so there's enough tender loving care going into each outbound effort.

More accounts per rep looks like leverage on a dashboard. If quality drops with it, it's just more motion.

What's your rep's real diligent capacity per week?

Slide 2: Reps work 200 to 300 accounts a week most diligently.
Slide 3: Expecting 500 to 1,000 a week at that quality is naive.
Slide 4: Raise volume too high and conversion pays the price.
Slide 5: Volume up, conversion down means the outcome barely moves.
Slide 6: Skyler's team targets about 500 to 600 accounts monthly.
Slide 7: Every outbound effort deserves real tender loving care.
Slide 8: Optimize for the outcome, not the activity count.

lesson.title: Volume Is Not the Outcome
takeaways: Rep capacity is finite: diligent work happens around 200 to 300 accounts a week, not 500 to 1,000.
Overloading reps drags conversion down, so extra volume rarely improves the outcome.
Set account loads so each outbound effort gets real care, then adjust for your own case.
lesson.exercise: Pull last quarter's data on accounts worked per rep versus conversion rate. Find where conversion starts to drop and set your account cap just below that point.

caption: More accounts, worse outcomes

angle: What Ethan and I work together on is we've got 10,000 accounts.
post_first_line: 10,000 target accounts. Good coverage on about 6,000.
linkedin_post:
10,000 target accounts. Good coverage on about 6,000.

The gap between those two numbers is where most outbound teams quietly lose.

Skyler Mickunas works with Ethan on exactly this problem. Too much AI and automation, and conversion rate pays the price. Too much manual effort, and a coverage gap opens up.

Everyone wants a fully automatic sniper rifle. Skyler's point: that does not exist.

So the two of them split the list. Ethan, on the growth and RevOps side, helps figure out that not every account in the 10,000 is equally attractive.

Skyler and Ethan then work out the top half, the tier 1 and tier 2 accounts, and how to get automated coverage over everything else.

As human headcount scales, more of tier 1 and tier 2 gets human attention.

The goal isn't to pick between automation and people. It's to decide which accounts earn each one.

How do you decide which accounts get human effort?
carousel: Slide 1: 10,000 target accounts. Realistic coverage on about 6,000.
Slide 2: Too much automation, and conversion rate pays the price.
Slide 3: Too much manual effort, and a coverage gap opens up.
Slide 4: The fully automatic sniper rifle does not exist.
Slide 5: Start by tiering: not every account is equally attractive.
Slide 6: Tier 1 and tier 2 get the human attention.
Slide 7: Everything else gets automated coverage.
Slide 8: As headcount grows, humans take on more of the top tiers.

lesson.title: Split Your Account List Between Humans and Automation
takeaways: Too much automation hurts conversion; too much manual work creates coverage gaps.
Not every account on a target list is equally attractive, so tier them.
Give tier 1 and tier 2 accounts human effort and automate coverage on the rest, shifting more to humans as headcount grows.
lesson.exercise: Take your target account list and estimate how many accounts your team can realistically cover by hand. Then mark the top half as tier 1 and tier 2, and decide how the remaining accounts will get automated coverage.
